brief.prompt: Netflix, 2014, migrating services from CentOS Linux to Ubuntu. A Cassandra database cluster moved to Ubuntu and write latency went up by over 30%; basic stats showed over 30% higher CPU consumption. Instances are EC2 Xen VMs. Steps and results: top(1) showed only the Cassandra database consuming CPU, no rogue Ubuntu service. execsnoop(8) (Ftrace version at the time) showed no short-lived processes. CPU flame graphs were collected on a CentOS instance and an Ubuntu instance in parallel so the time-of-day traffic mix matched. Java stacks were broken in both (pre -XX:+PreserveFramePointer era), only one or two green frames instead of a tower of Java methods. That breakage accidentally merged the os::javaTimeMillis() calls into one block instead of scattering them as thin stacks: 30.14% in the middle of the Ubuntu flame graph, 32.1% total after searching. os::javaTimeMillis calls gettimeofday(2), entering tracesys() and syscall_trace_enter/exit(). Two theories: (A) syscall tracing enabled on Ubuntu (auditing? apparmor?), (B) fetching time is slower on Ubuntu via a library or kernel/clocksource change. Frame widths favored A. Caveat: profile used perf(1) with software cpu-clock soft interrupts, not hardware NMI, because it is a Xen guest, so interrupts-disabled kernel paths and all hypervisor time are invisible. Ubuntu showed a vDSO frame with the syscall still above it, because Xen pvclock did not support vDSO then. Colleagues had not hit it and the internet had nothing on os::javaTimeMillis, clocksource, tracesys, Ubuntu, EC2, Xen. Write the investigation narrative for an engineering blog read by systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: Follow-on to a 2014 Netflix investigation where a Cassandra cluster on Ubuntu/EC2-Xen was burning about a third of its CPU inside os::javaTimeMillis(). No existing microbenchmark for that call existed, so one was written: TimeBench.java loops 100,000,000 times calling System.currentTimeMillis(), with a comparison against 87362 and a println inside the loop so the compiler will not optimize the loop away (which slows the test slightly). Run under shell time(1). CentOS: real 0m12.989s, user 0m3.368s, sys 0m18.561s. Ubuntu: real 1m8.300s, user 0m38.337s, sys 0m29.875s. Per-call cost is about 0.13 us on CentOS and 0.68 us on Ubuntu, Ubuntu 5x slower. A C version calling gettimeofday(2) directly, compiled -O0 to keep the loop, gave similar results; short benchmarks like this can be disassembled to confirm the compiler did what you expected. Second experiment: /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/available_clocksource listed xen, tsc, hpet, acpi_pm; current was xen, matching the pvclock_clocksource_read() frame in the flame graph. Echoing tsc into current_clocksource took effect immediately: TimeBench then ran real 0m3.370s, user 0m3.353s, sys 0m0.026s, over 20x faster than before and nearly 4x faster than CentOS. At roughly 33 ns per call the loop instructions themselves inflate the number; partially unrolling the loop would tighten it. TSC reads time with a single RDTSC instruction and works through vDSO with no syscall. TSC was historically avoided over clock-drift concerns; a processor engineer met at a conference said tsc had been stable for years but knew of no public reference. Combined with Netflix's fault-tolerant cloud, that was enough to try tsc in production. Production graphs showed write latencies drop 43%, slightly better than CentOS, and os::javaTimeMillis() fell to 1.6% with only a vdso frame above it. Write the experimentation-and-fix section of an engineering blog post for systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: Netflix case study, later summarized at Kernel Recipes 2017. A microservice team doing metrics ingestion updated their base OS image (BaseAMI) and then claimed ZFS was eating over 30% of CPU capacity. The engineer asked to help had worked on ZFS internals at Sun Microsystems and did not believe it: unless badly misconfigured, ZFS cannot consume that much CPU. He checked anyway. Atlas, the cloud-wide monitoring tool, showed 38% of CPU time in sys, highly unusual for Netflix cloud workloads. Rather than SSH in for mpstat(1) and perf(1), he used Netflix's flame graph fetch tooling (Vector, later FlameCommander). The flame graph showed two orange kernel towers, left and right. The left tower was arc_reclaim_thread; the right entered spl_kmem_cache_reap_now(), another ZFS memory-freeing path, probably contending on the same locks. Background: the ZFS Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) is the filesystem's main memory cache; arc_reclaim_thread runs arc_adjust() to evict and to maintain a free-memory threshold, periodically or when woken by low memory. A known past cause of arc_reclaim_thread CPU burn was a tiny record size such as 512 bytes creating millions of buffers, but the default is 128 Kbytes and nobody should tune below 8 Kbytes. First theory: a new infrastructure project using ZFS for containers, churning containers and therefore filesystems. The team said they were not using containers, then said they were not using ZFS at all. df -h, mount and zfs list showed no ZFS filesystems mounted, on two instances. /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats showed every counter at zero: hits 0, misses 0, all of them. Root cause found by reading source and change history: a multilist performance feature had split ARC lists one-per-CPU to cut lock contention, and eviction picked a list at random using a cryptographically-secure random number generator; the flame graph paths led to get_random_bytes() and extract_entropy(). ARC was detecting low system memory, randomly selecting a zero-sized list at expensive cost, then finding nothing to do. Filed as ZFS issue #6531; the first fix had arc_reclaim_thread bail out earlier when ZFS was unused. Write the case-study narrative for an engineering blog read by systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: A short Netflix debugging story. A colleague, Vadim, spotted something odd in a CPU flame graph of a TensorFlow workload: an unusual orange kernel tower amounting to 10% of total CPU time in page faults. Context on why that matters: at Netflix, 10% of CPU time somewhere unexpected is a large, costly issue across thousands of server instances, and flame graphs get used to chase down even 1% items. The stack traces showed the faults came from __memcpy_avx_unaligned(), memcpy faulting in data segment mappings. That makes sense early in a process's life when segments and heap are fresh and unmapped, but this process had been up for hours and RSS page-fault growth should have dwindled. Processes sometimes fault heavily because they call mmap()/munmap() to add and remove memory; eBPF tracing with mmapsnoop.py showed no such activity. Searching the flame graph for madvise showed 0.8% of CPU, and madvise() was calling zap_page_range(), which was causing the faults. Reading kernel mm/advise.c confirmed madvise() calls zap_page_range() for the MADV_DONTNEED flag (kprobes/tracepoints on sys_madvise() flags would have worked too). Diagnosis: a premature optimization gone bad, the allocator calling dontneed on pages it actually did need, dropping the virtual-to-physical mapping, which a page fault then had to restore. The allocator was jemalloc, selected by a configure option. Vadim rebuilt with glibc and the problem was fixed. Initial testing showed only a 3% win, verifiable in the new flame graph, against a hoped-for 10%. Write the case-study post for an engineering blog read by systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: Netflix, December 2018, kernel 4.4.0-1072-aws, 16-CPU instance. A service team hit a performance issue that coincided with a high rate of paging. The microservice managed and processed large files, encrypting them and storing them on S3. Files around 100 Gbytes took hours to upload; files as large as 40 Gbytes took only minutes. Atlas, the cloud-wide monitoring tool, showed a high rate of pageins during the large uploads; pageins are disk I/O where a page of memory is read in from disk, and are normal for many workloads. Investigation began with the 60-second performance checklist. iostat -xz 1 during a large upload: device xvdb at roughly 734 to 750 r/s, about 91,656 to 92,152 rkB/s, avgrq-sz about 246 to 250, avgqu-sz about 25, r_await about 33 to 34 ms, %util pegged at 100%; CPU showed roughly 14.8% user and 24 to 30% iowait. Read requests are the ones apps wait on; writes may not be, due to write-back caching. An r_await of 33 ms is highish and looks like queueing, and the I/O are largeish at about 128 Kbytes (rkB/s divided by r/s). Next, biolatency -m from bcc, an eBPF tool giving a latency histogram, in case averages hid device-level outliers: 8,139 I/O in the 32-63 ms bucket, 1,620 in 16-31 ms, 176 in 64-127 ms, 95 in 128-255 ms, 61 in 256-511 ms, 93 in 512-1023 ms, 83 in 0-1 ms. Most I/O between 16 and 127 ms with some outliers reaching 0.5 to 1.0 s, but the earlier queueing explains it: not a device issue, a workload issue. Then bitesize from bcc to check I/O sizes for anything odd: process name java, 1,682 I/O in the 128-255 Kbyte bucket and only tens elsewhere, matching iostat. Write the opening diagnosis section of a rough case-study post for systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: Second half of a Netflix case study on a file-processing microservice whose 100-Gbyte S3 uploads took hours while 40-Gbyte ones took minutes. Memory evidence: free -m on the problem instance showed total 64,414 MB, used 15,421, free 349, buff/cache 48,643, available 48,409, swap 0. So a 64-Gbyte memory system with 48 Gbytes sitting in the page cache and only 349 MB free. That plus the file sizes suggested a theory: 100-Gbyte files bust the page cache while 40-Gbyte files fit. Confirmation came from cachestat, an experimental tool written for Ftrace and since ported to bcc/eBPF, which reports page cache statistics. On the 100-Gbyte upload, cachestat showed hit ratios of 74.1%, 9.7%, 6.5%, 12.0%, 34.5%, 7.0%, 11.1% per second, with misses running from 632 up to 23,341, BUFFERS_MB 17 and CACHE_MB about 48,000. Ratios in the upper 90s are what you want to see; this is cache busting, because the 100-Gbyte file does not fit in 48 Gbytes of page cache, so misses turn into disk I/O. Control test on a 32-Gbyte file upload: cachestat showed 100.0% hit ratio with 0 misses across every second sampled (hits 33,424 to 65,158), BUFFERS_MB 41, CACHE_MB about 33,680; free -m showed used 18,421, free 11,218, buff/cache 34,773; iostat showed almost no disk I/O. The smaller file is processed entirely from memory however many passes it takes, without re-reading from disk. Recommended fixes: quickest is a larger-memory instance that fits the 100-Gbyte files; developers can also rework the code with the memory constraint in mind, for example processing parts of the file rather than making multiple passes over the whole thing. Closing context: cachestat was the killer tool but is still experimental, built under the constraints of low overhead and Ftrace function-profiler only. At the LSFMMBPF 2019 keynote in Puerto Rico, with Linux mm kernel engineers present, the argument was made that these statistics are commonly enough needed that they belong in /proc; the engineers pointed out real challenges in providing them properly, and page cache counters are hot-path so adding them is not free. Write the diagnosis-and-recommendation section of a rough case-study post for systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: A 20-year history piece on frame pointers, written in March 2024. The x86-64 ABI defines %rbp as a base pointer to a stack frame, the frame pointer, and external profilers and debuggers (Linux perf, eBPF) walk stacks with it, feeding flame graphs. But the ABI has a footnote calling the use optional: %rsp can index into the frame instead, saving two instructions in the prologue and epilogue and freeing one general-purpose register. In 2004 gcc developer Roger Sayle patched the i386 backend to default to the equivalent of -fomit-frame-pointer -ffixed-ebp on 32-bit targets. i386 had only four general-purpose registers, so freeing %ebp took it from four to five; Sayle also cited wanting to beat Intel's icc compiler and a belief that debuggers of the day were unaffected since they had other stack-walking techniques. The change was then applied to x86-64 as well, which had over a dozen registers. Eric Schrock, then at Sun, wrote in November 2004 that adding a 17th general-purpose register on amd64 opens no new world of compiler optimizations, that you are only saving a highly-optimized pushl/movl sequence, that leaf routines never establish a frame anyway, and that given the cost in lost debuggability it hardly seemed worth it, concluding that it gets out of control when people start compiling /usr/bin without frame pointers. That is what happened on Linux: /usr/bin, /usr/lib, and application code. Consequence: stack walking stops at the libc layer, producing partial stacks missing application frames that group together on the left of a flame graph, 15% of samples in one example. Off-CPU flame graphs suffer worse, being dominated by libc read/write and mutex functions. In 2014, joining Netflix, the author found Java's lack of frame pointer support broke all application stacks, developed a JVM c2 compiler fix that Oracle reworked into -XX:+PreserveFramePointer in JDK8u60, then compiled his own libc with frame pointers for production and worked with Canonical on a prebuilt libc6-prof. Write the historical narrative section of a technical blog post for systems and performance engineers.

brief.prompt: Material on the measured cost of enabling frame pointers, from production rollout work at Netflix between roughly 2015 and 2020, plus the case made to Fedora. Overhead of adding frame pointers to everything (libc and Java) was usually less than 1%, with one exception at 10%. That 10% outlier was an unusual microservice generating stack traces over 1000 frames deep via Groovy, over 3000 deep before inlining, deep enough to break Linux's perf profiler, whose prior limit was 128 frames; Arnaldo Carvalho de Melo of Red Hat added the kernel.perf_event_max_stack sysctl specifically for that Netflix workload. It was also a virtual machine without low-level hardware profiling, so no cycle analysis could confirm the 10% was frame-pointer-caused. Other attributes of that microservice: over 1 Gbyte of instruction text, possibly flying close to the edge of hardware cache warmth. Its developers ran a flame graph canary instance at first, then enabled frame pointers across the whole microservice because the wins outweighed the 10%. Others have reported around 1% and around 2%. Microbenchmarks are worst-case, hitting 10%, because they run a small function in a loop and extra prologue instructions can spill it out of L1 cache warmth or across a cache line. The Python scimark_sparse_mat_mult benchmark reached 10%; Andrii Nakryiko of Meta found the cause was a large function where gcc switched from %rsp offsets to %rbp-relative offsets, which took more bytes to store, since fixed, letting Python re-enable frame pointers by default. Against those costs: frame pointers have found performance wins ranging from 5% to 500%. The BPF Performance Tools book, page 40, records that the gain from frame pointer omission in production was usually under one percent and often too close to zero to measure. Recommended method for judging regressions: PEBS-based cycle analysis, or active benchmarking, because degrading a single hot function will happen to the next developer who adds code anyway, so the change gets unfairly blamed. Write the overhead-analysis section of a technical blog post for systems and performance engineers.
